messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented, Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Margaret is a 78-year-old graphic designer, married and still working part-time from the home studio she built in the basement of the house she and her husband bought fifty years ago. Two years ago, during a late-summer wildfire that swept through their county, she was alone in that studio when the evacuation order came too late. The fire had jumped the highway. She could see smoke pouring under the door at the top of the basement stairs—the heavy oak door that led to the kitchen. She ran up, but the wind had sucked the door shut and the metal latch jammed. She remembers pounding on it, screaming for her husband who was at the grocery store, then the sound of the door rattling in its frame as the fire trucks arrived and someone finally forced it open from the outside. That door—its slam, its shudder, the way it sealed her in—has never stopped echoing.

Now Margaret cannot bear the sound of any door opening or closing abruptly. When her husband comes home and lets the front door swing shut, her chest tightens and she feels the heat of that afternoon on her skin. She has taken to sitting in the living room where she can see the front door at all times, and she has asked him to open and close it slowly, without letting it catch. He tries, but sometimes he forgets, and the sharp click sends her heart racing. She knows it is irrational—she is not trapped now—but that knowledge does nothing to stop the feeling that the fire is happening again, that she is back in the smoke and the panic. At other times she can recall the event exactly, but the memory feels flat, almost as though it happened to someone else, and she wonders if she has gone numb. Then, without warning, the memory will snap into the present: she is once again pounding on the door, the smoke stinging her eyes, and she cannot convince herself that it is over.

The fire itself was contained within a few hours, but the aftermath has been slow and corrosive. Margaret’s neighbourhood was spared, yet she lost something less tangible. She had always believed that if you prepared carefully, stayed calm, and followed the rules, you would be safe. That belief is gone. She now watches the weather alerts with a vigilance that exhausts her, and she has started cleaning and reorganising her studio repeatedly—rearranging her drafting table, wiping down her monitors, stacking her sketchbooks in precise piles—because for a few minutes the orderliness pushes the dread aside. But the relief never lasts, and afterward she berates herself for wasting time. She also finds herself dwelling, sometimes for hours, on how the disaster could have been prevented: if the county had cleared more brush, if the evacuation routes had been announced sooner, if she had kept a crowbar by the basement door. The dwelling does nothing to change anything, but she cannot stop.

One of the hardest daily reminders comes from conversations with her neighbours or the news. Any mention of someone losing a loved one in a disaster—a family in California who lost a child, a widow who lost her husband in a hurricane—stops her cold. The talk does not directly remind her of a loss she suffered; she and her husband survived unharmed. But the injustice of it, the randomness, feels like a personal accusation. She has come to believe that the world is fundamentally dangerous, that no amount of preparation matters, and that what happened to her—the terrifying moments of entrapment—was deeply unfair, and nothing has been done about it. No one was held accountable for the poor planning, and the county still has not improved the emergency alerts. That sense of injustice gnaws at her more than the fear sometimes.

The smell of alcohol is another unexpected trigger. During the evacuation, a firefighter who had been directing traffic smelled strongly of liquor—Margaret recalls it distinctly as he helped her out of the house. She never learned if he was drinking on duty, but now the scent of beer or whiskey, whether from a neighbour’s barbecue or a passerby, yanks her back into that moment of helplessness. She avoids walking past the local pub, and she has asked her husband not to drink at home, which has created a quiet strain between them. He complies, but she knows he resents it, and she feels guilty, yet she cannot make herself tolerate the odour.

Her attempts to push the memory away have taken another form: she tries to erase it by deliberately not thinking about it, by refusing to say the word “fire” out loud, by changing the subject when anyone brings up natural disasters. It does not work. The memory stays, sometimes unreal, too extreme to have happened to her—a story that belongs to a different person. The effort of suppression has made her more tired, less focused at work. She is a graphic designer, and her projects require concentration; recently she missed a deadline because she spent an hour cleaning her studio instead of finishing a layout. Her client was understanding, but Margaret felt a deep shame.

What finally brought her to seek help was the door. Last week, her husband slammed the kitchen cabinet door—not the basement door, just a cabinet—and she found herself on the floor, her hands over her ears, sobbing. She decided then that she could not keep living this way, jumping at every sound, scrubbing her house into a false safety, running from a memory that never stays buried. She is hoping that talking about it will make the memory feel like it really is over, and not happening right now. But she is also afraid that if she lets herself feel the full weight of that afternoon, she will break apart—that the numbness will vanish and the terror will flood in and never stop.
